paras: The lynching of Three-Fingered Jack and Grizzly Dan was the killing of two men, Elias or Jack Ingalls and Dan Griscomb, in the woods four miles from Durango, Colorado, reported in April 1882. Wire reports alleged that the sheriff and other prominent men were among the lynchers and that the bodies were cut down and secretly buried.

The two men were known by nicknames, Ingalls as "Three-Fingered Jack" and Griscomb, described as his "pal," as "Grizzly Dan." The wire called them "notorious desperado[es]" but named no crime or charge against them, and no report gives the race of either man.

According to the dispatch, the men were lynched in the woods four miles from Durango; no report gives the date, the hour, or where they were seized. Their bodies were cut down within fifteen minutes, which suggests hanging, and were then secretly buried. It was "alleged that the Sheriff and other prominent men were members of the lynching party," while a shorter version of the item attributed the killing to "masked vigilantes."
No report of an inquest, arrest, or official inquiry into the sheriff's alleged part appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers only as a one-paragraph wire item, run on 21 April 1882 in news-summary columns of the Kenosha Telegraph, the Owosso Times and the True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan. The Owosso Times cut it to one sentence about the sheriff and "prominent citizens," and on 26 April the Hand County Press in Dakota reduced it further to "Two notorious desperadoes were lynched by masked vigilantes at Durango." None of these papers commented on the killing, and each placed it among unrelated briefs; the Kenosha copy printed Ingalls's name as "Logalls."

The wire reported two men called 'notorious desperado[es]' lynched in the woods by a 'lynching party' of the sheriff 'and other prominent men' (A4) or by 'masked vigilantes' (A5), with the bodies secretly buried; the label points to a summary-justice pretext, though no specific charge was printed. No text gives either man's race.
All four reports (A2-A5) are versions of one wire paragraph; no local Colorado account, inquest or follow-up was found.
